ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was a cross-sectional case control study with a single measurement timepoint and was approved by the Ethical Committee of the University of Luebeck (2025-164) on 5/15/2025.
Participants were informed that they would subsequently perform the activities.
For this study, participants with CSP and pain-free controls were recruited.
All participants had to be ≥18 years old and have sufficient knowledge of the German language to understand the provided study information and the questionnaires.

Exclusion criterion for both groups was uncorrected vision impairment as participants were required to clearly see the presented visual stimuli or if they reported any severe diseases interfering with pain and fear perception (e.g. anxiety, depression).

Participants with CSP were recruited from different orthopedic and physiotherapy outpatient clinics in Northern Germany in consultation with the practitioners and by displaying posters and sharing flyers.
Painfree participants were recruited at the university campus and via social media and personal contact.
Eligible participants were informed about study aims and procedures by members of the research team.
After deciding to participate, they provided written informed consent.
Participants were asked to fill out the informed consent form and patient-reported outcome questionnaires, first.
Additionally, participants were asked not to speak and to breathe normally during the measurement.
To increase the threat anticipation during picture presentation, the participants were told that they would have to perform the displayed movements immediately after the experiment.
In fact, no movement performance was required, and participants were debriefed about the purpose of the instruction at the end of the session.
Three participants were excluded due to synchronization failure.
Features with more than 50% missing values or data available for fewer than 80% of participants were excluded.
All participants provided their informed consent.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The sample size estimation was based on a 3x2 repeated-measures ANOVA (CONDITION X GROUP) for detecting an interaction effect of group and condition in the psychophysiological outcome measures (pupil dilation, electrodermal activity, heart rate, respiratory rate). The calculation was used as an a priori approximation for the planned mixed-effects analyses. It did not represent a multivariate power analysis across all outcome measures. CONDITION refers to (1) baseline measure, (2) mean of psychophysiological responses to the most feared movement picture and (3) mean of psychophysiological responses to the least threatening movement picture and GROUP stand for (1) healthy participants or (2) people with CSP. The calculation was conducted in G*Power using an effect size of f=0.295, based on skin conductance findings of Díaz-Sáez et al., 2021 [17], an alpha level of 0.05, a power of 0.80, three repeated measurements, and a correlation among repeated measures of 0.5. In Díaz-Sáez et al., autonomic responses were assessed following motor imagery or movement observation in people with chronic low back pain and pain-free participants, rather than continuously during picture presentation as in the present study. The effect size was considered an approximate planning value. This yielded a minimum total sample size of n=22 (i.e., 11 participants per group). Given the uncertainty in transferring the effect size from a different population and experimental paradigm, this estimate served as an approximate lower bound rather than the recruitment target. We therefore aimed to recruit 30 participants per group (i.e., n=60 in total) to obtain more precise estimates and to accommodate potential data loss in psychophysiological and eye-tracking recordings.

Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p≥0.05", Sentence = "The ratings did not show any significant effects for repetition and group or their interaction (p≥0.05) (Table 4, Figure 5)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. For this study, participants with CSP and pain-free controls were recruited.
All participants had to be ≥18 years old and have sufficient knowledge of the German language to understand the provided study information and the questionnaires.

Exclusion criterion for both groups was uncorrected vision impairment as participants were required to clearly see the presented visual stimuli or if they reported any severe diseases interfering with pain and fear perception (e.g. anxiety, depression).

Participants with CSP were recruited from different orthopedic and physiotherapy outpatient clinics in Northern Germany in consultation with the practitioners and by displaying posters and sharing flyers.
Painfree participants were recruited at the university campus and via social media and personal contact.
Eligible participants were informed about study aims and procedures by members of the research team.
After deciding to participate, they provided written informed consent.
Participants were asked to fill out the informed consent form and patient-reported outcome questionnaires, first.
Additionally, participants were asked not to speak and to breathe normally during the measurement.
To increase the threat anticipation during picture presentation, the participants were told that they would have to perform the displayed movements immediately after the experiment.
In fact, no movement performance was required, and participants were debriefed about the purpose of the instruction at the end of the session.
Three participants were excluded due to synchronization failure.
Features with more than 50% missing values or data available for fewer than 80% of participants were excluded.
All participants provided their informed consent.

text.text: Fear of movement-related pain (FMRP) contributes to disability in chronic musculoskeletal pain.
However, psychophysiological correlates of activity-specific threat appraisal during FMRP-eliciting tasks remain insufficiently understood.
This cross-sectional study examined self-reports and psychophysiological responses to shoulder-straining daily activities in individuals with chronic shoulder pain (CSP) and pain-free controls.
Participants observed six pictures depicting shoulder movements selected as highly or minimally threatening.
Each picture was presented five times in random order.
Participants were informed that they would subsequently perform the activities.
Following each presentation, participants rated anticipated fear, urge to avoid, and expected harmfulness.
Electrodermal activity, pupil diameter, heart rate, respiratory rate, and gaze behavior were recorded continuously.
Self-reports differentiated between highly and minimally threatening activities and were higher in the CSP group (p≤0.001).
SCL differentiated between threat categories, with more pronounced responses in the CSP group (pBH-corrected=0.008; f² =0.029).
Within the CSP group, SCL correlated weakly with ratings of fear (ρ=0.137; pBH-corrected=0.008) and harmfulness (ρ=0.127; pBH-corrected=0.013), but not urge to avoid (ρ=0.022; pBH-corrected=0.763).

Pupil dilation (pBH-corrected≤0.001; f² =0.039) and gaze behavior (pBH-corrected=0.006; f² =0.067) differed between individual pictures in the CSP group but did not consistently differentiate the predefined threat categories.
Heart rate and respiratory rate showed no consistent effects.

This is the first shoulder-specific picture-viewing paradigm combining selfreports with several psychophysiological measures and the first study to examine pupil dilation as a potential correlate of FMRP.
The findings suggest that electrodermal activity may reflect sympathetic arousal related to activity-specific threat appraisal during FMRP-eliciting picture-viewing.
People with chronic pain are often afraid of movements they believe to cause harm or worsen their pain [79].

text.text: According to the fear-avoidance model [79], psychological factors such as pain-related fear and avoidance behavior are important contributors to pain-related disability.
text.formatted: According to the fear-avoidance model <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">[79]</ref>, psychological factors such as pain-related fear and avoidance behavior are important contributors to pain-related disability.

text.text: The model proposes that pain-related worrying (often referred to as pain catastrophizing [13]) and negative affectivity, driven by threatening illness information, or individual tendencies to interpret pain as harmful or threatening, heighten the chance of acquiring fear of pain, fear of movement or fear of (re)injury, subsequently leading to avoidance behavior.

text.text: The resulting outcomes may include the development of depression and functional disability [34, 78].
text.formatted: The resulting outcomes may include the development of depression and functional disability <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">78]</ref>.

text.text: This vicious circle reinforces both the levels of pain intensity and unpleasantness as well as functional disability [14, 47, 78].

text.text: Consequently, fear of movement-related pain (FMRP) plays an important role in musculoskeletal pain chronification [24, 32, 57] and may predict pain-related disability better than pain intensity [15, 83].
text.formatted: Consequently, fear of movement-related pain (FMRP) plays an important role in musculoskeletal pain chronification <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">57]</ref> and may predict pain-related disability better than pain intensity <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">83]</ref>.

text.text: However, FMRP does not manifest uniformly across all movements but depends on how individual activities are appraised with regard to their anticipated pain, harm, and behavioral consequences (e.g., avoidance of the activity).

The fear-avoidance model [28, 79] suggests that FMRP is acquired through classical conditioning, where an initially neutral movement (conditioned stimulus) is associated with pain or injury (unconditioned stimulus).

text.text: FMRP can also be learned through indirect pathways, such as observational or instructional learning [22, 61].

text.text: Shoulder pain is a major individual and societal health problem [1, 81] and among the three most common musculoskeletal complains next to neck pain and low back pain [23, 35].

text.text: FMRP is predominantly measured by rather generalizing patient-reported outcome measurements [32, 52], with limited data on psychophysiological processing of activity-specific threat appraisal during experimental FMRP paradigms.

text.text: Among psychophysiological measures, autonomic measures, including heart rate (variability), respiratory rate and electrodermal activity, have received considerably less attention [17, 56, 73].

text.text: Although autonomic responses represent established indicators of emotional arousal and defensive responding [5, 31, 80], little is known about whether different autonomic systems provide comparable or complementary information during experimentally elicited FMRP.

text.text: In particular, pupillometry has not yet been investigated in this context despite its established role as a measure of sympathetic arousal in anxiety, fear conditioning, and pain anticipation research [9, 12, 19, 25, 36].

text.text: Therefore, the aim of the present study was to investigate psychophysiological responses during an experimentally FMRP-eliciting picture-based movement observation paradigm in people with CSP and pain-free controls.

Specifically, we examined whether pupil dilation provides additional information on activity-specific threat appraisal alongside autonomic measures used in prior research, including electrodermal activity, heart rate and respiratory rate.

text.text: The study was a cross-sectional case control study with a single measurement timepoint and was approved by the Ethical Committee of the University of Luebeck (2025-164) on 5/15/2025.
The study protocol was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/26UGD).
text.formatted: The study protocol was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (<ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/26UGD">https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/26UGD</ref>).

text.text: For this study, participants with CSP and pain-free controls were recruited.
Pain-free controls were selected to be comparable in age to participants with CSP (±5 years) and to achieve a broadly comparable gender distribution at group level.
All participants had to be ≥18 years old and have sufficient knowledge of the German language to understand the provided study information and the questionnaires.
Participants with shoulder pain were included if the shoulder pain persisted for ≥3 months, as defined for a chronic pain syndrome [7, 75].
text.formatted: Participants with shoulder pain were included if the shoulder pain persisted for ≥3 months, as defined for a chronic pain syndrome <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">75]</ref>.

text.text: Exclusion criterion for both groups was uncorrected vision impairment as participants were required to clearly see the presented visual stimuli or if they reported any severe diseases interfering with pain and fear perception (e.g. anxiety, depression).

Further, participants with CSP were excluded if the shoulder pain had a neurological origin (e.g. pain due to paraplegic subluxation) and pain-free controls were excluded if they had a history of chronic pain or experienced severe pain in the last 24h.

Participants with CSP were recruited from different orthopedic and physiotherapy outpatient clinics in Northern Germany in consultation with the practitioners and by displaying posters and sharing flyers.
Painfree participants were recruited at the university campus and via social media and personal contact.
Both groups were additionally recruited in sports clubs.
Inclusion and exclusion criteria were verified at the beginning of the session.
Eligible participants were informed about study aims and procedures by members of the research team.
After deciding to participate, they provided written informed consent.

The sample size estimation was based on a 3x2 repeated-measures ANOVA (CONDITION X GROUP) for detecting an interaction effect of group and condition in the psychophysiological outcome measures (pupil dilation, electrodermal activity, heart rate, respiratory rate).
The calculation was used as an a priori approximation for the planned mixed-effects analyses.
It did not represent a multivariate power analysis across all outcome measures.

CONDITION refers to (1) baseline measure, (2) mean of psychophysiological responses to the most feared movement picture and (3) mean of psychophysiological responses to the least threatening movement picture and GROUP stand for (1) healthy participants or (2) people with CSP.

The calculation was conducted in G*Power using an effect size of f=0.295, based on skin conductance findings of Díaz-Sáez et al., 2021 [17], an alpha level of 0.05, a power of 0.80, three repeated measurements, and a correlation among repeated measures of 0.5.
text.formatted: The calculation was conducted in G*Power using an effect size of f=0.295, based on skin conductance findings of Díaz-Sáez et al., 2021 <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>, an alpha level of 0.05, a power of 0.80, three repeated measurements, and a correlation among repeated measures of 0.5.

text.text: In Díaz-Sáez et al., autonomic responses were assessed following motor imagery or movement observation in people with chronic low back pain and pain-free participants, rather than continuously during picture presentation as in the present study.
The effect size was considered an approximate planning value.
This yielded a minimum total sample size of n=22 (i.e., 11 participants per group).
Given the uncertainty in transferring the effect size from a different population and experimental paradigm, this estimate served as an approximate lower bound rather than the recruitment target.

We therefore aimed to recruit 30 participants per group (i.e., n=60 in total) to obtain more precise estimates and to accommodate potential data loss in psychophysiological and eye-tracking recordings.

From the 58-pictures set from Tozzo et al. (2024), three of the six movement pictures that were rated highest in previous publications using the Avoidance of Daily Activities Photo Scale (ADAP; [2, 3]) and the Fear of Daily Activities Photo Scale (FDAP; [55]) regarding arousal [72], fear and urge to avoid [55, 74] were chosen ('pushing'; 'carrying on shoulder, hip and back'; 'lifting').

text.text: Lighting in the room was adapted to a moderate illumination, aiming for an initial detection confidence in pupil detection of >0.9 after calibration.

text.text: The color images were presented at eyelevel on a screen placed at a 60cm distance from the participant.
The images were fixed at the center of the screen.

The screen resolution was 2560×1600 on a 13.3-inch true tone retina display, allowing for an automatic adjustment in tone and brightness and therefore reduction of variability in how participants perceive contrasts due to external lighting changes.
All pictures were adapted to a size of 4:3 and had a standardized color profile (sRGB IEC61966-2.1), brightness and contrast.
Participants were asked to fill out the informed consent form and patient-reported outcome questionnaires, first.

Afterwards, electrodes and chest belt for the assessment of electrocardial data, electrodermal activity and respiratory data were attached and the eye tracker glasses for the pupillometry assessment were individually adjusted.
Following, the participant was placed in front of the screen to get used to the display of the stimulus material and for the calibration of the eye tracker.
Before the picture presentation started, the participant sat and rested for at least 5min to control for increased autonomic system reactions due to physical activity.
Additionally, participants were asked not to speak and to breathe normally during the measurement.
To increase the threat anticipation during picture presentation, the participants were told that they would have to perform the displayed movements immediately after the experiment.
In fact, no movement performance was required, and participants were debriefed about the purpose of the instruction at the end of the session.

For the main data collection, psychophysiological measurements were initially recorded for a 1min resting baseline phase with a grey screen background and an introduction text saying "Following, we will show you pictures of activities impacting the shoulder joint.
Please imagine performing the shown movements while you are seeing them." [70].
text.formatted: Please imagine performing the shown movements while you are seeing them." <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">[70]</ref>.

text.text: Following, a white fixation cross on grey background screen was displayed for 5s, followed by a 6s movement-picture onset.
Each picture was followed by ratings of fear, urge to avoid and expected harmfulness on a VAS-scale, before the presentation of the next fixation cross.
Each loop consisted of all 6 pictures (3 most threatening, 3 least threatening) that were shown in a random order.
The experiment consisted of 5 blocks (loops) of stimuli, as recommended by Steinhauer et al. (2023; [70]).

Respiration data were collected via an elastic belt positioned on the rip cage.
The data were recorded at 200Hz using the OpenSignals software (© 2025 PLUX Biosignals).

In the CSP group, the pain and disability related to daily activities was measured at baseline with the Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (SPADI) with 5 items in the pain subscale and 8 items in the disability subscale [1].

Sociodemographic data were collected from both groups and included age, gender, self-reported psychiatric disorders, and medication use (anxiolytics, antidepressants, and analgesics).

In addition, participants with CSP reported pain duration, medical diagnosis, previous shoulder surgery, their individually most feared movement, the perceived origin of their shoulder complaints (e.g., repetitive work-related movements or overhead sports), and whether the affected shoulder was the right or left and dominant or non-dominant side.
Pain-free controls additionally reported any previous shoulder pain or chronic pain that was no longer present at the time of participation.

Pupil diameter data and gaze position (fixation) data collected by the Pupil Core eye tracking system were preprocessed to reduce artifacts, following procedures recommended by Steinhauer et al. (2023; [21,70]) and Mathôt & Vilotijević (2022; [37]).

(2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">[21,70]</ref>) and Mathôt & Vilotijević (2022; <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>).

text.text: Although the eye cameras recorded data at 120Hz per eye, data from both eyes were resampled onto a common 60Hz time grid before further preprocessing, as the two eye cameras have independent, non-aligned timestamps.
Pupil samples were marked as artifacts if they contained missing values or had a confidence score below 0.6.
Missing samples were replaced by linear interpolation along the time axis on the full continuous recording, restricted to interior gaps of up to 0.5s.
No extrapolation beyond the first or last valid sample was performed.
Interpolation was conducted before segmenting the recording into analysis windows.
Additionally, a linear detrending was performed separately for each eye across the full recording to remove slow drifts and increase the emphasis on phasic pupil responses.
A bilateral pupil signal was constructed, based on signal quality, by computing the mean if the signal of both eyes was usable.
If only one eye provided a usable signal, that signal was retained (10.2% of recordings).
No recordings had unusable signals from both eyes.
Further, data driven clipping of the signal was performed with 0.1% and 99.9% quantiles of the valid pupil samples.
Pupil dilation was computed as the difference from mean pupil diameter in the experimental condition to the pre-trial baseline condition [36, 62].
text.formatted: Pupil dilation was computed as the difference from mean pupil diameter in the experimental condition to the pre-trial baseline condition <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">62]</ref>.

text.text: Pupil diameter reflected the two-dimensional detection diameter in camera pixels.
The data analyzed therefore comprised detrended pixel residuals rather than raw pupil diameter in millimeters.
To additionally analyze gaze patterns, fixations and saccades were manually identified frame by frame using the world-camera video of the eye tracker.
Fixations with a duration of ≥100ms were included.
No upper duration threshold was applied.
Predefined areas of interest (AOI) are the shoulders of the people displayed in the pictures as well as the faces.
The detection of fixations in the AOI was done manually by using the world camera video of the eye tracker.
Time to first fixation (TFF) in AOI and first fixation duration (FFD) were analyzed [18, 82].
text.formatted: Time to first fixation (TFF) in AOI and first fixation duration (FFD) were analyzed <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">82]</ref>.

text.text: The electrodermal activity, electrocardial and respiratory data were preprocessed using the NeuroKit2 tool [33].
text.formatted: The electrodermal activity, electrocardial and respiratory data were preprocessed using the NeuroKit2 tool <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: The electrodermal activity data signal was smoothed, a low pass filtering was applied, the data were decompositioned in tonic and phasic components and a skin conductance response detection was performed, aligned with contemporary recommendations [4, 69].
text.formatted: The electrodermal activity data signal was smoothed, a low pass filtering was applied, the data were decompositioned in tonic and phasic components and a skin conductance response detection was performed, aligned with contemporary recommendations <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">69]</ref>.

text.text: A signal of exactly 0µS was reported as electrode dropout, and signal plausibility was determined using a threshold of 200µS.
ECG and respiration data were filtered, and an R-peak-detection was performed.
For the ECG data, interbeat intervals were calculated and the heart rate was estimated.
Data plausibility was confirmed in a heartbeat range of 40-200bpm.
ECG artifacts were additionally identified based on clipping at the sensor limits (±1.47mV) and flatline periods, defined as a rolling standard deviation below 0.05mV over 1s.

For respiration data, artifacts were identified based on clipping at the sensor limits (±1.50V), flatline periods with a rolling standard deviation below 0.01V over 10s and samples deviating by more than 6 standard deviations from the participant-specific mean.
The three recording systems (PsychoPy, OpenSignals, Pupil Labs) ran on independent clocks.
For each participant, a device-specific time offset into PsychoPy time was therefore computed; the pupil offset was additionally verified against the first and last stimulus event.
Three participants were excluded due to synchronization failure.
Quality thresholds for the data were defined upfront (Table I, supplementary material).

text.text: Trial windows were defined as 12s (3s pre + 6s stimulus + 3s post).
Inter-trial-intervals were flowing as there was no predefined time window for the self-reported ratings, adding to the 5s rest period before the new trial window started.
However, only the 6s picture-presentation period was included in hypothesis testing.
Features were calculated in 1s analysis windows.
An analysis window was considered valid if it contained <50% missing data.
text.formatted: An analysis window was considered valid if it contained <50% missing data.

text.text: Windows exceeding this threshold were assigned‚ missing feature values' and excluded from subsequent averaging.
No whole trial was removed as a unit.
Across the 8820 analyzed picture-presentation windows, 0.70% of skin conductance responses, hear rate and respiration data as well as 0.62% of pupil data were missing.
At trial level, all stimulus windows were missing in 9 of 1470 trials for the SCL, heart rate and respiration rate measures as well as in 1 of 1470 trials for the pupil data.
All psychophysiological data were baseline-corrected using the mean of the 3s pre stimulus period to account for lighting changes during the study session.
The sociodemographic data and the results of the PROMs were analyzed descriptively.
After assessing for normal distribution, the scores of the PROMs were correlated to explore associations between different selfreport measures.

Candidate features were automatically extracted from the continuous psychophysiological recordings.

These features represented characteristics of the physiological responses within the pre-defined analysis windows for each participant, picture presentation, and measurement modality (i.e., mean, auc, min, max).
An automated quality audit was then conducted to identify features with sufficient data completeness for the analyses.
Features with more than 50% missing values or data available for fewer than 80% of participants were excluded.
Within clusters of highly correlated features (|r|>0.90), only the feature with the fewest missing values was retained.

text.text: On activity level, effect sizes for both SCL responses (p BH-corrected ≤0.004; f² =0.031) slightly improved and pupil dilation (pBH-corrected≤0.001; f² =0.038) stayed the same after adding the TSK and PCS scores as covariates in the linear mixed models, but revealed significant results only in the CSP group as well.

However, implementing the TSK and PCS scores as covariates lead to significant results for the SCL responses in the comparison of threat categories across groups (pBH-corrected=0.006; f² =0.017) and in the CSP group (pBH-cor-rected=0.026; f² =0.017).
The expected differences in psychophysiological responses were partly supported.
Tonic electrodermal activity (e.g., SCL) differentiated between individual activities and predefined threat categories, and revealed distinct patterns compared to baseline between groups.
Pupil diameter differentiated between individual activities only, whereas heart rate and respiratory rate did not consistently distinguish between activities or threat categories.
However, these findings did not consistently support the expected differences in psychophysiological response patterns between groups.

The paradigm successfully elicited activity-specific threat appraisal, reflected by consistently higher fear, urge to avoid, and harm ratings for highly threatening compared with less threatening activities, with stronger responses in participants with CSP.
No consistent repetition effects were detected.

Together, these findings demonstrate that the used picture-based movement observation paradigm can reliably elicit pre-existing FMRP while revealing distinct psychophysiological response patterns across autonomic measures.

Although most experimental evidence from movement observation paradigms originates from low back pain populations [56], substantially fewer studies include neck pain [27, 48] or shoulder pain [55, 72, 73].

text.text: The present study extends existing shoulder-related research by combining activity-specific threat ratings with several psychophysiological measures, including pupillometry, in CSP.

Experimental research has repeatedly shown that pain-related fear generalizes beyond movements previously associated with pain to perceptually or functionally similar activities, even when these activities have never been directly paired with pain or injury [42, 43].
text.formatted: Experimental research has repeatedly shown that pain-related fear generalizes beyond movements previously associated with pain to perceptually or functionally similar activities, even when these activities have never been directly paired with pain or injury <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43]</ref>.

text.text: Excessive generalization may result in objectively safe activities being appraised as potentially harmful, thereby promoting persistent avoidance and disability [79].
text.formatted: Excessive generalization may result in objectively safe activities being appraised as potentially harmful, thereby promoting persistent avoidance and disability <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">[79]</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, the higher fear, urge to avoid, and harm expectancy ratings for low-threat pictures observed in CSP may reflect broader generalization of threat appraisal towards daily activities rather than heightened responses to a few particularly threatening movements alone.

Within the fear-avoidance model, threatening illness information is assumed to shape expectations about pain and harm, thereby facilitating activity-specific threat appraisal and subsequent avoidance behavior [79].
text.formatted: Within the fear-avoidance model, threatening illness information is assumed to shape expectations about pain and harm, thereby facilitating activity-specific threat appraisal and subsequent avoidance behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">[79]</ref>.

text.text: These mechanisms closely resemble contemporary concepts of nocebo effects, which are increasingly recognized as clinically relevant in people with musculoskeletal pain, including CSP [29, 30, 65].

text.text: Inadvertently communicated threatening information may therefore increase FMRP and contribute to persistent avoidance and disability.

The differentiated psychophysiological responses observed in the present study suggest that picture-based movement observation may provide a standardized framework to examine such information-induced effects, although threatening information was not explicitly manipulated.

Among the investigated psychophysiological measures, SCL differentiated both between individual activities and between predefined threat categories and was weakly associated with self-reported fear and harm expectancy ratings in participants with CSP.

These findings are consistent with a previous movement observation study in low back pain demonstrating increased skin conductance during a FMRP-eliciting paradigm [17] and extend this evidence to CSP.

text.text: As electrodermal activity primarily reflects sympathetic activation associated with emotional arousal and defensive reactions [11, 69], the present findings suggest that autonomic arousal accompanies the appraisal of an activity's anticipated threat value.

text.text: The observed correlations with self-reports were small, indicating a weak correspondence between self-reported appraisals and SCL.
The interpretation of SCL differences also requires consideration of the depicted activities and the experimental instructions.
Highly threatening activities (e.g. pushing) may involve greater anticipated physical effort, which could contribute to arousal during movement observation [10, 16].

text.text: These aspects may help explain the observed responses, although their respective contributions were not examined separately.
Pupillometry revealed a different response pattern.
Pupil diameter is strongly influenced by sympathetic activation and has been widely used as an indicator of arousal in anxiety research, fear conditioning and pain anticipation [9, 25, 36].

text.text: In contrast to SCL, pupil dilation differentiated between individual activities but not between the predefined threat categories.
These findings suggest that pupil responses may be sensitive to subtle differences in the appraisal of individual activities.

As pupil diameter reflects sympathetic and locus coeruleus-noradrenergic activity and the intensity of emotional arousal [36, 49], individual activities within the same predefined threat category may differ in their capability to elicit arousal.

text.text: Pupillometry may therefore provide complementary information on activity-specific threat appraisal and represents a promising addition to psychophysiological measures in experimental FMRP research.
Franklin et al. (2018; [19]) previously examined pupil diameter and gaze behavior during viewing of threatening back-related images.
text.formatted: Franklin et al. (2018; <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>) previously examined pupil diameter and gaze behavior during viewing of threatening back-related images.

text.text: The present study extends this research by investigating pupillometry during shoulder-related movement observation in CSP and relating physiological responses to activityspecific threat ratings.
Gaze behavior also differed between individual pictures, providing preliminary information about visual attention during movement observation.
These measures therefore characterize responses to individual activities, although their differentiation of the predefined threat categories was less consistent than that of SCL and self-reports.
In contrast, heart rate and respiratory rate did not consistently differentiate between activities or threat categories.

While both measures have previously been shown to respond during experimentally elicited FMRP [17], methodological differences, including stimulus presentation and experimental procedures, limit direct comparisons.

text.text: In people with CSP, Tozzo et al. (2026; [73]) found reduced parasympathetic modulation during shoulder movement observation compared with pain-free controls.

text.text: As heart rate variability reflects a different aspect of cardiovascular regulation than mean heart rate, these findings suggest that cardiovascular responses to movement observation may depend on the measure examined.
Taken together, the present findings indicate that experimentally elicited FMRP is not reflected uniformly across self-reports and psychophysiological measures.
Instead, the observed response patterns suggest that different assessment modalities capture complementary aspects of activity-specific threat appraisal.
According to appraisal theories of emotion, emotional responses emerge from an individual's evaluation of anticipated consequences of a situation rather than from the stimulus itself [20, 46, 76].
text.formatted: According to appraisal theories of emotion, emotional responses emerge from an individual's evaluation of anticipated consequences of a situation rather than from the stimulus itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">76]</ref>.

text.text: Hence, observing daily activities may initiate an appraisal process in which anticipated pain, expected harm, perceived capability and behavioral relevance of the activity are evaluated.
Depending on the outcome of this appraisal, physiological and behavioral response systems may become activated to varying degrees.
This framework provides a plausible explanation for the different psychophysiological response patterns observed in the present study.
Self-reports directly capture the conscious evaluation of anticipated threat, whereas SCL appears to reflect sympathetic arousal associated with this evaluation.

Rather than identifying a single psychophysiological marker of FMRP, the present findings support examining multiple psychophysiological assessment modalities, while their complementary contribution remains to be established.

This interpretation is also consistent with our previous work demonstrating that a picture-based questionnaire primarily elicits task-or activity-specific threat appraisal that is not entirely consistent with general FMRP [55].
text.formatted: This interpretation is also consistent with our previous work demonstrating that a picture-based questionnaire primarily elicits task-or activity-specific threat appraisal that is not entirely consistent with general FMRP <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref>.

text.text: While FMRP represents the broader pain-related construct, experimentally elicited activity-specific threat appraisal may provide access to one of its underlying mechanisms under standardized laboratory conditions.
Neither self-reports nor psychophysiological responses changed across repeated picture presentations.
For physiological measures, correction against the immediately preceding baseline may obscure habituation affecting both baseline and picture-viewing periods.
One possible explanation for the absence of consistent repetition effects is that merely observing the activities did not provide an opportunity to test anticipated harmful consequences.
In exposure-based interventions, the absence of expected harm may lead to expectancy violation, supporting corrective learning and reducing fear-related avoidance and disability [22, 77].
text.formatted: In exposure-based interventions, the absence of expected harm may lead to expectancy violation, supporting corrective learning and reducing fear-related avoidance and disability <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">77]</ref>.

text.text: The present paradigm may provide a standardized approach to examine whether activity-specific threat appraisal changes following such experiences.

The present findings support the use of picture-based movement observation paradigms as a standardized experimental approach to investigate activity-specific threat appraisal in individuals with pre-existing FMRP.
Future studies could assess anticipated physical effort and manipulate instructions, including threatening information, to distinguish their contributions to psychophysiological responses.
Comparing heart rate and heart rate variability within the same paradigm and examining responses during movement execution or expectancy violation may clarify their responsiveness.

Integrating self-reports, behavioral, psychophysiological and neurophysiological measures could help determine their complementary contributions and to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of FMRP and the mechanisms contributing to fear-related disability in chronic musculoskeletal pain.
This study has several strengths.
To our knowledge, it is the first to evaluate pupillometry as a psychophysiological correlate of experimentally elicited FMRP.

Furthermore, combining self-reports with electrodermal activity, pupillometry, heart rate, respiratory rate and gaze behavior enabled simultaneous assessment of multiple response systems under standardized experimental conditions.
Some limitations should be considered.
First, movement observation cannot fully reproduce the sensory and motor experience of performing potentially threatening activities.
Consequently, the present findings cannot be directly transferred to real-life movement behavior.
Second, participants with CSP reported only moderate levels of self-reported FMRP (measured by TSK, FABQ and PCS scores), which may have attenuated group differences in psychophysiological responses.

Finally, autonomic responses are influenced by multiple factors beyond FMRP, including general emotional arousal and attentional processes, as well as technical sensitivity issues when recording them.
Therefore, psychophysiological measures should be interpreted in relation to the experimental context rather than as specific biomarkers of FMRP.
The present study supports picture-based movement observation as a feasible approach to experimentally elicit activity-specific threat appraisal associated with pre-existing FMRP in people with CSP.
While SCL emerged as the most robust psychophysiological correlate, pupil dilation provided additional information on sympathetic arousal during the appraisal of individual daily activities.

Together, these findings support the use of complementary psychophysiological assessment modalities to improve the mechanistic understanding of FMRP and to further advance experimental research on fear-related disability in chronic musculoskeletal pain.
